clusters.name: Your stepfather Desmond arriving and your parents' separation, 1987
clusters.reason: Around 1987, when you were in secondary school, three shifts pile up: your distance from Desmond as an obstacle rather than support, your pull toward your father for his notice, and the onset of anxiety as you made the city chess squad and found yourself out of your depth. Your stepmother's brief separation from your father over starting a family sits in the same months, a strain in the household during your early teens; no one else's shifts show then.

clusters.name: Your grandfather Gordon's death and your move to the rebuilt house, 1989–1994
clusters.reason: Around 1989 to 1994, your shifts pile up and circle around a rebuild of the household. Your father's reconciliation with his own father opened the period in early 1989; within months you had moved to a cramped rental on Quarry Lane and then the rebuilt Hollin Road house with your stepfather's children, and your late nights and absorption in music began. Your grandfather Gordon died in June 1991 as you started at the conservatory. You leaned hard on your roommate Rafe, then collided with him once a wrist injury stopped your playing in October 1991; you fell into isolation and drug use. Your grandmother Winifred underwent surgery for thyroid cancer within a year or so of his death. A disastrous audition and a failed pursuit of your father's notice sit in the same stretch. Your functioning fell, your anxiety rose, and you cycled through relationships of fusion and conflict. You raced through your degree and found your footing again in 1994, when the period settles.

clusters.name: Your separation from Joelle and your move into therapy, 1998–1999
clusters.reason: In 1998 and 1999, you were bonded with Joelle and playing the best you ever had, winning competitions for a couple of years. Your insomnia began getting in the way around the same time; sleepless nights before concerts plagued you though you practised hard. The relationship separated in July 1999, and you started with a therapist in August. Two shifts count in these months—your symptom rising as insomnia and your functioning rising as your performing reached its peak—and the separation and therapy sit among them; no one else's shifts show then.

clusters.name: Your grandmother Winifred's cancer diagnosis and your depression after Marisol, 2001–2004
clusters.reason: Around 2001 to 2004, the family was shaken by your grandmother Winifred's diagnosis of bowel cancer in 2001 or 2002, the same months you were running out of steam for performing and felt less content by the month. You had a disastrous audition for the national orchestra in your home town and were done with performing. You grew distant from your parents and friends, left Thornbury for Gull Harbour, then met Marisol at a winter party in early 2003 and moved with her to Fenwick. You separated within the year and sank into a deep depression once you were back in Thornbury that winter. Your grandmother spent her final months in your parents' home. You could not face your family, but relied on friends—Corbin, Dale, and Hamish—and took a long walk with Silas, who took no side. Corbin spoke with your father several times during your stay. Your functioning fell through this stretch; your anxiety rose; and your distance from your parents deepened even as you turned toward friends. You began swimming laps in January 2004, returned to your therapist Victor Halloran, and requested help from your parents with therapy costs. Your grandmother died in February 2004, and your functioning began to climb again. The period settles as you took up therapy and began to recover.

clusters.name: Your grandmother Lorna's death and your cutoff from your mother, 2008
clusters.reason: Around 2008, your grandmother Lorna died in January. Within months you were at Alder Creek building with Silas before nursing school. You grew too drained for conversation with your mother; she pressed you to visit despite your repeated refusals, and the visit went wrong—she could not get inside. You stopped speaking to your mother when you moved to Marlow Sound that August to begin nursing school, and the silence held for roughly a year. Your aunt Imogen had a stroke with months of rehabilitation. Your relationship with your mother shifted from distance to cutoff; your anxiety rose as you could not face contact with her; and the pressure built between you until you left. No one else's shifts show in these months.

clusters.name: Your marriage to Wren and her family's press on you, 2017–2019
clusters.reason: Around 2017 to 2019, you married Wren in March 2017, and within months your contact with your mother eased off slightly once Wren came along. Your cousin Alice was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis in her forties in October 2017. Your sister Tara married and had a baby on the way. By October 2019, Wren's brother Leo and his family had returned nearby. Around the same time, Wren became swamped with a street party, a fundraising dinner, and a drive to the lake for her mother's retirement party. You overfunctioned, laying out a plan too strictly to settle her; she speaks with her father and brother all day and they are fused, hearing everything that happens to one of them. Once the weekend had a plan, she settled and the dinner went well. But you awoke from the small hours at the lake weekend with no more sleep and could only pull back as the others rose. Your anxiety rose around her family; you feel you don't belong there. Your sleep is at its worst around her family occasions, followed by long quiet drives home. Your anxiety is down when your job steadies and you started a sleeping pill, but rises again as you constantly feel you ought to be driving your projects forward. You have aimed for shorter, more regular calls with your mother to soften the distance that piles up. Multiple shifts in anxiety, functioning and relationship pile up in these months around the press of her family and the strain of belonging.
